q1340: Much of daily life runs on automatic habits, reaching for food, a snack or a phone without thinking. These habits are driven partly by the brain's reward system, which uses dopamine to push us toward whatever has felt good before. Pausing a desire on purpose interrupts that loop. A short food fast brings hunger signals that can feel uncomfortable, but many people find they also sharpen attention, which can be turned toward prayer. A screen fast reduces the constant stream of small rewards, and over days the mind often feels calmer and less scattered. Replacing the time with Scripture gives the space a purpose. Drinking water and breaking the fast gently protects the body. Medical advice first matters, because fasting is not safe for everyone, and a non-food fast is a fully valid choice for many.
q1341: God gave us appetites as good gifts, but He did not design us to be ruled by them. Fasting helps put desires back in their right order, with love for God first and other good things after. It reflects His wisdom, because a person who can say a gentle "not now" to food or screens becomes freer and steadier in every part of life. It also reflects His grace. God does not ask us to fast to prove our worth. Christ has already done that. He invites us to fast so that we discover He is enough, even when our stomachs or our feeds are empty. Ending with thanks reminds us that the food and the phone are His gifts too. Fasting done gently and wisely trains the heart toward freedom, clarity and closer fellowship with Him.
q1342: The Bible often links rest and quiet breathing with trust in God. Through Isaiah He says, "In returning and rest shall ye be saved, in quietness and in confidence shall be your strength" (Isaiah 30:15). David describes his own soul settling like a child resting with its mother: "Surely I have behaved and quieted myself, as a child that is weaned of his mother" (Psalm 131:2). Psalm 62:5 says, "My soul, wait thou only upon God." Jesus invites the weary to come to Him and find rest for their souls (Matthew 11:29). Scripture does not see the body as separate from faith. Calm, unhurried breathing can be a way of practising that quiet confidence, letting the body join the soul in resting on God instead of bracing against life.
q1343: Your heart does not beat like a metronome. It speeds up a little as you breathe in and slows as you breathe out, and the size of this natural swing is called heart-rate variability. Higher variability is generally linked with a more flexible, resilient nervous system. Research on resonance breathing suggests that around six breaths a minute, about five seconds in and five or six out, is the pace where heart rhythm, breathing and blood-pressure reflexes line up most strongly, so the swing becomes larger and smoother. Keeping the breath soft and quiet avoids over-breathing, which can cause dizziness. Practised for five to ten minutes twice a day, studies suggest this kind of breathing may improve resting heart-rate variability over weeks, helping the body recover from stress more quickly and making calm easier to reach.
q1344: God filled creation with rhythm. Day follows night, seasons turn, tides rise and fall, and inside us the heart and lungs keep their own patterns. He designed these rhythms to work together, so that when we slow our breath, the heart responds and the whole body leans toward peace. This shows His care in the details. He built a calming system into us that does not need special equipment, only time and attention. It also reflects His character as a God of order and peace, not confusion. Practising this breathing twice a day is a small act of agreeing with His design, choosing His pace instead of the world's rush. Over time, a body that is often tense can learn steadiness again, and that steadiness gives space for clearer thinking, kinder words and deeper prayer.
q1345: Scripture is not shy about the body expressing what the soul feels. "And David danced before the LORD with all his might" (2 Samuel 6:14), leaping and spinning as the ark came home. The psalmist praises God, "Thou hast turned for me my mourning into dancing" (Psalm 30:11), and calls God's people to praise His name in the dance (Psalm 149:3). Ecclesiastes 3:4 reminds us there is "a time to mourn, and a time to dance." The Bible shows people trembling in fear and leaping for joy, like the healed man at the temple gate who went "walking, and leaping, and praising God" (Acts 3:8). God meets us in bodies, not only in ideas. Letting the body move freely after stress can be a way of handing tension back to Him and receiving His release.
q1346: When we feel threatened, the body prepares to fight or flee. Stress hormones such as adrenaline and cortisol rise, muscles tighten and energy floods in. In modern life the threat is often an email or an argument, so we do not run or fight, and that energy can stay trapped as tension. Many animals visibly shake after danger passes, and body-based therapists use similar movements to help people leave the stress state. Bouncing on your heels and shaking out your hands, arms, shoulders and legs uses some of that stored energy and signals that the danger is over. Loosening the jaw and sighing aloud releases muscles that often hold stress. Standing still afterwards and breathing slowly lets you notice the shift. Repeated over weeks, this can teach the body to return to calm more readily after hard moments.
q1347: God made us with a stress system that is meant to switch on, deal with danger and then switch off again. The trouble is not the alarm itself but staying stuck in it. By giving us bodies that can shake, move and dance, He provided a natural way to complete the cycle and come back to rest. This reflects His kindness in making us whole beings, where the body is not an enemy but a partner in healing. It also reflects His joy. The God who made David's dancing feet is not embarrassed by our movement. Shaking it out can feel silly at first, but it is honest. It admits we carry stress, and it lets go. Over time, this simple habit helps body and soul move from bracing to peace, ready to meet God and others freely.
q1348: The Bible often connects where we look with where our hope lies. "I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help. My help cometh from the LORD" (Psalm 121:1-2). Isaiah tells the weary and fearful, "Lift up your eyes on high, and behold who hath created these things" (Isaiah 40:26), turning their gaze to the vast night sky. Psalm 19:1 says the heavens declare the glory of God, and Paul urges us to set our affection on things above (Colossians 3:2). Again and again, Scripture invites people narrowed by fear to widen their view. When the eyes take in the whole horizon, the heart is reminded that God is bigger than the one problem filling our sight, and that His care surrounds us on every side.
q1349: The eyes and the nervous system are closely linked. When we feel threatened or very focused, vision tends to narrow, almost like a spotlight, which helps us track one thing but keeps the body alert. When we feel safe, vision tends to relax and widen, taking in more of the scene. Researchers who study vision and stress suggest that deliberately widening the gaze, while keeping the eyes still, may help nudge the body away from alarm. Noticing the edges of your sight on the left, right, top and bottom engages this wider mode. Relaxing the forehead, face and jaw releases muscles that tense with focus. A long, slow out-breath adds a calming signal through the vagus nerve. Practised regularly, such as once an hour, it gives your body frequent small resets throughout a demanding day.
q1350: God designed our eyes not only to see but to help us feel safe. He made the wide horizon, the open sky and the far-off hills, and He made us able to rest when we take them in. This reflects His wisdom in linking body and soul so closely that even softening our gaze can quiet fear. It also reflects His heart as Protector, whose care is all around us, not only straight ahead. When our focus is narrow, we can feel alone with a problem. When our view widens, we remember there is room, space and help beyond it. Looking slowly around the room at the end is a reminder to return to life calmly. Over time, the habit of lifting and widening our eyes becomes a habit of lifting our hope to God.
q1351: Jesus saw the tiredness of His disciples. After a busy season of ministry, when so many were coming and going that they had no time even to eat, He said, "Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while" (Mark 6:31). Rest is woven into God's pattern from the beginning, when each day of creation closes with "the evening and the morning" and the seventh day is set apart. The shepherd of Psalm 23 leads His sheep beside still waters (Psalm 23:2), and Psalm 46:10 calls us to be still. Isaiah 30:15 says, "in quietness and in confidence shall be your strength." Scripture shows that short pauses are not laziness. They are part of a life lived with God, where we stop, breathe and remember that the work is His before it is ours.
q1352: The brain produces electrical rhythms called brain waves. When we close our eyes and relax while awake, alpha waves usually increase, a pattern linked with calm, restful alertness. Opening the eyes and focusing on a task tends to reduce them again. Short eyes-closed breaks give the visual system a rest and lower the flood of information the brain must process. Research also describes attention residue, where part of our mind stays stuck on the last task after we move on. A three-minute pause with breathing that slows naturally can help clear that residue, so we return more focused. Letting thoughts drift without chasing them, or picturing a peaceful scene, lowers mental effort. Stretching afterwards wakes the body gently. Built into the day, these breaks may reduce fatigue and help concentration last longer.
q1353: God did not design us to work without stopping. He built pauses into creation and into our bodies, from the beat of the heart, which rests between each contraction, to the brain, which renews itself when we close our eyes. This reflects His wisdom as a Creator who knows our limits better than we do. He remembers that we are dust and does not demand machine-like output. It also reflects His grace. Rest is a gift we receive, not something we have to earn by finishing everything first. A three-minute pause in the afternoon is a small act of trust, saying that the world will not collapse while we breathe. Over weeks, these little rests can protect us from burnout, help us think more clearly and keep our hearts soft toward God and people.
q1354: Scripture pictures God as a Shepherd who sees when His sheep need rest. "He maketh me to lie down in green pastures: he leadeth me beside the still waters" (Psalm 23:2). David writes, "I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep: for thou, LORD, only makest me dwell in safety" (Psalm 4:8). Psalm 127:2 warns against rising early and staying up late in anxious toil, "for so he giveth his beloved sleep." Jesus calls, "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest" (Matthew 11:28). The Bible shows that rest is something God gives and protects. Lying down in His care is not a waste of time. It is a way of trusting that He holds us and our responsibilities while we let our bodies recover.
q1355: When we are stressed or tired, the body often stays slightly braced, with tight muscles, raised heart rate and elevated stress hormones, even when we are not doing anything. Deep guided rest, such as a slow body scan, helps release this. Lying on your back with a pillow under your knees eases strain on the lower back. Breathing out slowly signals safety through the vagus nerve. Moving attention from toes to head and softening each part relaxes muscle groups one by one, and studies suggest such relaxation can lower heart rate and stress markers. Picturing God's care adds emotional safety. Some research suggests this kind of rest may support sleep quality and focus. Practised regularly, the body learns to drop into relaxation more easily. Rolling to one side and sitting up slowly protects blood pressure and avoids dizziness.
q1356: God made us with two great modes in the nervous system, one for action and one for rest and repair. Healing, digestion and renewal happen mainly in the second. If we never truly rest, the body cannot fully restore itself. By designing deep relaxation into us, God gave a way to recover even on days when sleep is short. This reflects His tender character. He is the Shepherd who makes us lie down, knowing we often will not stop on our own. It also reflects His faithfulness, because rest is safe only when someone trustworthy is watching over us, and He neither slumbers nor sleeps. Fifteen minutes of lying still before Him can renew energy, steady emotions and remind us that we are loved, not for what we produce, but because we are His.
q1357: The Bible opens in a garden and closes with a river and a tree of life, and in between it keeps pointing to creation as a witness to God. "The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament sheweth his handywork" (Psalm 19:1). Jesus told anxious people to look at the birds and "consider the lilies of the field, how they grow" (Matthew 6:26-29). Job says the beasts, birds and earth itself can teach us that the hand of the LORD has made them all (Job 12:7-10). Paul writes that God's power and nature are clearly seen in what He has made (Romans 1:20). Time outdoors is not a break from God. It is time spent in His handiwork, where He speaks through beauty, order and the quiet care He shows for every sparrow and flower.
